entry.title: Why SLIs Matter More Than SLOs
entry.summary: SLOs get all the attention. I want to argue that your SLIs are more important. Here's the thing: an SLO is a number you pick. 99.9% uptime. 300ms p95 latency. Whatever. It's a decision. An SLI is what you're actually measuring. Is it the right signal? Does it reflect user experience? Is it gamed by caching? Those questions matter more than the target. '99.9% of healthcheck requests return 200.' Looks great on paper. Means nothing to users. Your healthcheck endpoint can be up while your actual API is broken. '99.x% of user-initiated checkout requests complete successfully within 5 seconds.' That signal tells you if the product works. Whatever target you pick, you're measuring the right thing. When your SLO is missed, does on-call get paged because a real user is suffering? If yes, your SLI is good. If no, you're measuring the wrong thing. Pick the SLI first. Pick the SLO second. Most teams do it backwards and wonder why their reliability work doesn't move the needle. Written by Dr. Samson Tanimawo https://novaaiops.com

entry.title: Por qué el "precio de lista" de una tienda no vale nada (y cómo construimos un tracker honesto)
entry.summary: En Argentina hay una jugada instalada: la tienda infla el precio de lista unos días antes de un Hot Sale y después te muestra un "-70% OFF" sobre ese número inflado. El descuento es de mentira, pero el cartel funciona. Construyendo (des)contamelo aprendimos algo que define toda la arquitectura: el precio que declara la tienda no es evidencia de nada. Si querés saber si algo bajó de verdad, no podés comparar contra el "precio anterior" que dice el comercio. Necesitás tu propio baseline. Guardamos el precio real de cada producto todos los días y armamos su historial. Cada señal se calcula contra nuestros snapshots, nunca contra el número que declara la tienda: Baja real: el precio actual está por debajo del mínimo/mediana de las últimas semanas. Mínimo histórico: la alerta más valiosa. Descuento dudoso: una "oferta" que no mejora nuestro historial reciente. Es la anti-señal que desenmascara el Hot Sale trucho. Precio real deflactado por inflación: en un país con inflación alta, un precio "igual" en pesos es en realidad más barato. Ajustamos con el IPC del INDEC. Cada tienda es distinta (VTEX, Tiendanube, Shopify, Magento, Salesforce Commerce, Empretienda…), pero el dominio no debería enterarse. Cada integración entra por una interfaz PriceSource, y ningún concepto de proveedor cruza la frontera del adapter. El dominio conoce Store, Product, PriceSnapshot — nunca "un producto VTEX". Regla dura que nos ahorró dolores: si un adapter no puede leer el precio con confianza, tira un error tipado. Nunca devolvemos un precio adivinado — un precio dudoso guardado contamina el historial para siempre. Un tracker que compara contra el precio de lista de la tienda es tan mentiroso como el cartel. La única forma de detectar una baja real es tener memoria propia. Eso hace (des)contamelo: pegás el link de un producto de cualquier tienda argentina, lo seguimos todos los días, y te avisamos por mail solo cuando el precio baja de verdad. Es gratis. Si querés ver cómo se ve el historial de un producto, está en descontamelo.com.

Retrieval-augmented generation is already the default context source, and provider-native retrieval has quietly overtaken the dedicated vector databases that define the category — yet a majority of enterprises have already watched their agents produce confident, wrong answers traced to missing or inconsistent context. A governed semantic layer is emerging as the fix, but most are still building it; the field is converging on hybrid retrieval; and even as provider-native tools lead in practice, a plurality say they intend to keep best-of-breed. entry.title: The agent evaluation gap: Enterprise AI organizations have a reality-alignment problem, not a coverage problem — and most are shipping to production anyway
entry.summary: Across 157 enterprises, organizations are granting AI agents more autonomy while trusting the evaluations meant to gate that autonomy less. Half have already shipped an agent that passed their internal evaluations and then failed a customer in production; only one in twenty fully trusts automated evaluation today; and the most-cited weakness is that evaluations do not align with real-world outcomes. Yet two-thirds already allow, or are actively engineering toward, deploying agent changes to production on automated evaluation alone — with no human in the loop. The result is an evaluation gap — the distance between how much autonomy enterprises are handing their agents and how far they trust the tests that are supposed to catch the failures. entry.title: Agentic orchestration: Enterprise AI organizations have a deployment problem, not a platform problem — and most are calling chatbots agents
entry.summary: Across 101 enterprises, agent orchestration is consolidating onto model-provider platforms — Anthropic’s Claude leads by a wide margin — chosen for the gravity of the underlying model and judged on reliable multi-step execution. But the ambition runs well ahead of the reality: most deployed “agents” are still chatbot wrappers, the control plane enterprises expect is deliberately hybrid to avoid lock-in, and real-time fiscal control over token burn remains the exception.
